subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Meta-Debate: Arguing About How to Argue
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Meta-Debate: Arguing About How to Argue usable.

hook.text: Two people are arguing. One uses data. The other uses moral principles.

buildup.text: Meta-debate: arguing about the rules, standards, & methods of argumentation itself. What counts as evidence?

discovery.text: Many seemingly irresolvable disagreements are actually meta-disputes: we agree on the facts but not on how to.

twist.text: 'The data says policy X works.' 'But it violates human rights.' Both are using valid frameworks – they just disagree.

climax.text: Resolution: explicitly name the framework disagreement. 'We agree on the facts.

punchline.text: Before you argue, agree on what would count as winning.

quiz.question: What is a meta-debate?
options: An argument about the rules, standards, and methods of argumentation itself

details.summary: A meta-debate is an argument about the rules, norms, or framework of the debate itself. Before you can resolve a disagreement, you often need to agree on what counts as evidence, what the question really is, and how to proceed.
details.whyItMatters: Many debates stall because participants are playing by different rules. Resolving the meta-debate unlocks the substantive one.
takeaways: Meta-debates address the rules of engagement, not the topic
Unresolved meta-disagreements make substantive debate impossible
Agreeing on terms and standards is often the hardest step

faq.question: What is a common example of a meta-debate in everyday life?
faq.answer: When one person argues with statistics and the other responds with personal stories, the disagreement is partly about what counts as evidence. Resolving that meta-question lets the real debate proceed.

faq.question: How do you initiate a meta-debate without derailing the discussion?
faq.answer: Pause and say something like 'Before we continue, can we agree on what would change each of our minds?' This frames the meta-question as cooperative rather than obstructive.
